questions.q: What does the book call the region around a magnet, or around a current-carrying wire, in which its magnetic effect can be felt, for example by the deflection of a compass needle?
questions.a: A magnetic field
o: A magnetic field
A magnetic pole
An electric circuit
A heating element

questions.q: Hamid's compass lies under a wire joined to a cell through a switch. He wonders whether it is the wire itself, and not the current in it, that turns the needle. Which observation settles that it is the current?
questions.a: The needle turns only while the switch is ON and swings back when it is OFF.
o: The needle turns only while the switch is ON and swings back when it is OFF.
The needle turns a little more when the wire is pressed closer to the compass.
The needle points in its old direction once the compass is lifted far away.
The wire feels slightly warm after the switch has been ON for some time.

questions.q: Which of these devices does the book give as a practical application of the magnetic effect of electric current?
questions.a: Electric bell
o: Electric bell
Electric kettle
Electric iron
Immersion rod

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A wire carrying an electric current can deflect a magnetic compass needle placed beneath it.
Reason (R): The magnetic field around a current-carrying wire disappears when the current stops flowing.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning or description in Column II.
Column I: I. Magnetic field  II. Magnetic effect of electric current  III. Compass needle  IV. Electric bell
Column II: A. A tiny magnet that deflects when a magnet is brought near it  B. A device that works on the magnetic effect of electric current  C. The region around a magnet or a current-carrying wire where its magnetic effect is felt  D. A conductor carrying current produces a magnetic field around it
questions.a: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B
o: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B
I-D, II-C, III-A, IV-B
I-C, II-D, III-B, IV-A
I-C, II-A, III-D, IV-B

questions.q: (a) Define the magnetic effect of electric current. (b) What happens to the magnetic field around a wire when the current stops flowing?
questions.a: (a) When an electric current flows through a conductor such as a wire, it produces a magnetic field around it; this is the magnetic effect of electric current. (b) The magnetic field disappears.
s: (a) Current through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it
(b) The magnetic field disappears when the current stops

questions.q: Rakesh's compass lies under a wire joined to a cell through a switch. He moves the switch to ON and leaves it ON for two minutes. His friend says, 'The needle will swing once and then go back to its original direction, even with the switch still ON.' (a) What will the needle actually do during the two minutes? (b) Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The needle stays deflected for the whole two minutes. (b) A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it for as long as the current flows; the field disappears, and the needle returns to its original direction, only when the current stops.
s: (a) The needle stays deflected while the switch is ON
(b) The field lasts as long as the current flows and disappears only when it stops

questions.q: A magnetic compass is placed beneath a wire that is connected to a cell through a switch. Answer briefly. (a) What happens to the compass needle when the switch is moved to ON? (b) What happens to the needle when the switch is moved back to OFF? (c) What does the movement of the needle tell us about the wire while current flows?
questions.a: (a) The needle gets deflected from its original direction. (b) The needle returns to its original direction. (c) The current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect, that is, it produces a magnetic field around it.
s: (a) Needle is deflected from its original direction
(b) Needle returns to its original direction
(c) The current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field (magnetic effect)

questions.q: Sunil, an electrician's helper in Warangal, has no tester lamp. He holds a magnetic compass just beneath each of three wires in turn, with the wire running along the needle, and notes: Wire A: the needle turns away and stays turned. Wire B: the needle does not move at all. Wire C: the needle turns away while its switch is ON and swings back when Sunil moves the switch to OFF. (i) to (iii): For each wire, say whether the compass shows that current is flowing in it. (iv) State what the compass needle is detecting around a wire that carries current.
questions.a: (i) Wire A: yes, current is flowing, because the needle is deflected. (ii) Wire B: no current is shown, because there is no deflection, so no magnetic effect. (iii) Wire C: current flows only while the switch is ON; when the switch is OFF the current stops and the needle returns. (iv) The compass needle, a tiny magnet, detects the magnetic field that the current produces around the wire.
s: (i) Wire A: deflection shows current is flowing
(ii) Wire B: no deflection, no current shown
(iii) Wire C: current flows only while the switch is ON
(iv) The needle detects the magnetic field produced by the current

questions.q:
Arya worked with a circuit of a cell in a holder, a switch and a long wire stretched just above a magnetic compass. No magnet and no other circuit was nearby. Read her five lab notes and, for each, say whether it can be correct, giving the reason from the chapter.
(a) 'With the switch ON, the needle deflected even with a sheet of cardboard between the wire and the compass.'
(b) 'With the switch OFF, the needle stayed deflected for five whole minutes.'
(c) 'I took the cell out of its holder, moved the switch to ON, and the needle deflected.'
(d) 'With the switch ON the needle pointed away from its original direction, and when I switched OFF it came back.'
(e) 'So the wire becomes a permanent magnet once current has passed through it.'
questions.a: (a) Can be correct: the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as cardboard. (b) Cannot be correct: with the switch OFF no current flows, the magnetic field disappears and the needle returns to its original direction. (c) Cannot be correct: without the cell no current flows, so there is no magnetic field to deflect the needle. (d) Correct: the needle deflects while current flows and returns when it stops. (e) Cannot be correct: the magnetic field exists only while current flows and disappears when it stops, so the wire is not a permanent magnet.
s: (a) Possible: magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic cardboard
(b) Not possible: no current when OFF, so the needle returns
(c) Not possible: no cell means no current and no field
(d) Correct: deflects with current, returns without
(e) Wrong conclusion: the field disappears when the current stops

questions.q: What is a current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet called?
questions.a: An electromagnet
o: An electromagnet
A bar magnet
A compass needle
A heating element

questions.q: Pooja's coil of insulated wire is wound on a rolled chart-paper tube. Joined to a cell, it deflects a nearby compass needle only a little. Without changing the cell or the number of turns, which change will make the deflection much more?
questions.a: Slide an iron nail into the paper tube.
o: Slide an iron nail into the paper tube.
Slide a thick copper rod into the paper tube.
Slide a wooden pencil into the paper tube.
Wrap a second layer of chart paper over the coil.

questions.q: How can the poles of an electromagnet be reversed?
questions.a: By changing the direction of the current in the coil
o: By changing the direction of the current in the coil
By adding more turns of wire to the same coil
By adding one more cell to the battery in use
By taking the iron nail out of the middle of the coil

questions.q:
Kiran's electromagnet, 40 turns of insulated wire on an iron nail joined to 1 cell, holds 3 iron clips. Read these predictions.
I. If he unwinds the coil to 20 turns and keeps the same cell, it will hold more clips.
II. If he joins the same coil to a battery of 3 cells, it will hold more clips.
III. If he turns the cell round, the poles of the electromagnet will be reversed, but this alone will not make it hold more clips.
Which of these predictions is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
II only
I, II and III

questions.q: True or False? 'Just like a bar magnet, an electromagnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. When the two ends of the coil, A and B, are tested one at a time with a magnetic compass, they are found to have opposite polarity: one end is a north pole and the other a south pole, just like a bar magnet.
s: States True
Compass test shows the two ends have opposite poles, north and south

questions.q: (a) Why do most electromagnets used in practical applications have an iron core? (b) What happens to the iron paper clips clinging to an electromagnet when the current is stopped?
questions.a: (a) An iron core makes the electromagnet stronger. (b) The clips fall off, because the coil loses its magnetic effect when the current stops.
s: (a) The iron core makes the electromagnet stronger
(b) Clips fall off as the magnetic effect is lost

questions.q: (a) Name the two changes that the book says can make an electromagnet stronger. (b) Harsh has only one cell and cannot get another. Which of these two changes can he still make to strengthen his electromagnet?
questions.a: (a) Increasing the electric current through the coil (for example, using a battery with more cells) and increasing the number of turns of the coil. (b) He can increase the number of turns of the coil, since that does not need another cell.
s: (a) Names more current and more turns
(b) Chooses increasing the number of turns

questions.q: End A of Rhea's nail electromagnet is a north pole. She claims: 'If I add two more cells to my battery, joined the same way as the first, end A will turn into a south pole.' Is her claim right? Explain.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. Adding cells joined the same way gives a larger current, which makes the electromagnet stronger (more deflection, more clips held). But the current still flows in the same direction, and the poles are reversed only when the direction of the current is changed, so end A stays a north pole.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
More cells give a larger current, so a stronger electromagnet
Poles reverse only if the current's direction changes; here it does not, so A stays north

questions.q:
In a school lab in Shillong, Dawa wound 50 turns of insulated wire on a rolled chart-paper tube and placed a magnetic compass near one end of the coil. She noted how far the compass needle turned from its resting direction in four set-ups.
Set-up 1: coil on the paper tube only, 1 cell: 15°.
Set-up 2: coil on the paper tube only, a battery of 2 cells: 30°.
Set-up 3: an iron nail slid into the tube, 1 cell: 60°.
Set-up 4: as in Set-up 3, but with the cell disconnected: 0°.
(a) In which set-up did the needle turn the most, and what was added in that set-up?
(b) Compare Set-ups 1 and 2. What changed, and what does the result show?
(c) Why did the needle return to its resting direction in Set-up 4?
(d) Without changing the cell or removing the nail, name one other change Dawa could make to get a larger deflection than in Set-up 3.
questions.a: (a) Set-up 3 (60°). An iron nail was added as a core, and an iron core makes the coil a much stronger magnet. (b) The number of cells changed from 1 to 2. The deflection doubled from 15° to 30°, showing that a larger current makes the electromagnet stronger. (c) With the cell disconnected no current flows, so the coil loses its magnetic effect and the needle returns. (d) Wind more turns of wire on the coil, because more turns make the electromagnet stronger.
s: (a) Set-up 3; the iron core makes it much stronger
(b) Cells 1 to 2: larger current, stronger electromagnet (15° to 30°)
(c) No current, so the coil loses its magnetic effect
(d) Increase the number of turns

questions.q:
Sahil tested electromagnets made of the same insulated wire and identical cells, and recorded how many iron clips each could hold.
Trial 1: 1 cell, 60 turns, iron nail core: 5 clips.
Trial 2: a battery of 3 cells, 180 turns, iron nail core: 26 clips.
Trial 3: 2 cells, 60 turns, no core (paper tube): 2 clips.
Trial 4: 1 cell, 120 turns, iron nail core: 9 clips.
Trial 5: 2 cells, 60 turns, iron nail core: 11 clips.
(a) Which two trials show the effect of the number of turns alone? (b) Which two trials show the effect of the number of cells alone? (c) Which two trials show the effect of the iron core alone? (d) Sahil compares Trial 1 with Trial 2 and says, 'Tripling the turns made my electromagnet more than five times stronger.' Explain why this comparison cannot show that. (e) In Trial 5, end A was a north pole. If Sahil turns the battery round so that the current flows the other way, what will end A become, and should the number of clips held change much? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Trials 1 and 4: only the turns change (60 to 120), and the clips rise from 5 to 9. (b) Trials 1 and 5: only the cells change (1 to 2), and the clips rise from 5 to 11. (c) Trials 3 and 5: only the core changes, and the clips rise from 2 to 11. (d) Between Trials 1 and 2 both the number of cells (1 to 3) and the number of turns (60 to 180) changed, so the rise from 5 to 26 clips cannot be put down to the turns alone. (e) End A becomes a south pole, because reversing the current reverses the poles. The number of clips should not change much, because the amount of current and the number of turns, which decide the strength, are the same.
s: (a) Trials 1 and 4
(b) Trials 1 and 5
(c) Trials 3 and 5
(d) Two things changed at once, so the effect of turns alone cannot be told
(e) A becomes south; strength about the same since current and turns are unchanged

questions.q: A crane's lifting electromagnet has no permanent magnet inside it. What makes it behave as a magnet?
questions.a: The electric current flowing through its coil
o: The electric current flowing through its coil
The steel load hanging below it
The heat produced in its coil
The steel cable of the crane

questions.q: In Sumana's exhibition model of a lifting electromagnet, what was used in place of the hook of a typical crane?
questions.a: An iron nail wrapped with a wire connected to a battery
o: An iron nail wrapped with a wire connected to a battery
A bar magnet tied firmly to the end of a string
A copper wire bent into the shape of a crane hook
A lemon cell joined by wires to a small bright LED

questions.q: At a ship-breaking yard in Alang, a crane's lifting electromagnet is switched ON just above a heap holding an iron pipe, a copper pot, an aluminium sheet and a steel bolt. (Copper and aluminium are not magnetic materials.) Which items does it lift?
questions.a: The iron pipe and the steel bolt only
o: The iron pipe and the steel bolt only
All four metal items in the heap
The copper pot and the aluminium sheet only
The iron pipe only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A crane's lifting electromagnet can pick up a steel girder that is not hooked or tied to it in any way.
Reason (R): A lifting electromagnet keeps working as a magnet even when no current flows through its coil.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A lifting electromagnet can be made able to lift heavier iron loads by increasing the electric current through its coil.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. A lifting electromagnet is an electromagnet, and a larger current through the coil produces a stronger magnetic field, so the electromagnet becomes stronger and can lift more.
s: States True
Larger current gives a stronger magnetic field, so a stronger electromagnet

questions.q: (a) What are lifting electromagnets? (b) How does a crane operator control a lifting electromagnet?
questions.a: (a) Strong electromagnets that may be hung from cranes to lift iron and steel objects. (b) By switching the current ON to lift the iron or steel objects and OFF to release them, since the magnetic field disappears when the current is off.
s: (a) Strong electromagnets hung from cranes
(b) Current ON to lift, OFF to release

questions.q: A factory's lifting electromagnet is rewired so that the current now flows through its coil in the opposite direction; the amount of current is the same. (a) What happens to the poles of the electromagnet? (b) Will it still lift steel objects? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The poles are reversed: the north end becomes south and the south end becomes north. (b) Yes. Iron and steel are attracted to either pole (in the coil activity, iron clips are attracted to both ends of the nail), and the strength depends on the amount of current and the number of turns, which are unchanged.
s: (a) The poles are reversed
(b) Still lifts: steel is attracted to either pole and the strength is unchanged

questions.q: Answer briefly about lifting electromagnets. (a) Name the two places where the book says lifting electromagnets are widely used. (b) Name the three jobs they do there with heavy metal items. (c) What kind of objects can they lift?
questions.a: (a) Factories and scrap yards. (b) They move, lift and sort heavy metal items. (c) Iron and steel objects.
s: (a) Factories and scrap yards
(b) Move, lift and sort
(c) Iron and steel objects

questions.q:
At a steel factory in Jamshedpur, the current in a crane's lifting electromagnet can be set to Low, Medium or High. The factory chart gives the heaviest steel load the magnet can hold at each setting: Low 300 kg, Medium 600 kg, High 900 kg. Today the operator must move a 250 kg steel plate, a 550 kg roll of steel sheet, an 850 kg steel girder and a 200 kg aluminium block.
(a) Why can the magnet hold a heavier load on High than on Low?
(b) To save electricity, she uses the lowest setting that is enough for each load. Which setting does she use for each of the three steel loads?
(c) Can she move the aluminium block with the magnet on any setting? Give a reason.
(d) Halfway to the store with the girder on High, could she turn the setting down to Low to save electricity? Explain using the chart.
questions.a: (a) On High a larger current flows through the coil, which makes a stronger magnetic field, so the electromagnet is stronger. (b) The 250 kg plate: Low (Low holds up to 300 kg). The 550 kg roll: Medium (more than 300 kg, up to 600 kg). The 850 kg girder: High (more than 600 kg, up to 900 kg). (c) No. Lifting electromagnets lift iron and steel objects; aluminium is not a magnetic material, so it is not attracted on any setting. (d) No. Low holds at most 300 kg and the girder is 850 kg, so the weaker magnetic field could not hold it and the girder would fall.
s: (a) Larger current, stronger magnetic field, stronger electromagnet
(b) Plate Low, roll Medium, girder High
(c) No: only iron and steel objects are lifted; aluminium is not magnetic
(d) No: 850 kg is more than the 300 kg Low can hold, so it would fall

questions.q:
Explain each of these five observations made at a scrap yard and in a school model, using what the chapter teaches about electromagnets and electric current.
(i) When the crane's magnet is switched ON above a heap, iron scrap rises but aluminium cans stay behind.
(ii) In the school model, a coil of 100 turns on an iron nail lifts more clips than a coil of 40 turns on the same kind of nail, joined to the same cell.
(iii) After the current in the coil is increased, the magnet lifts an iron block it could not lift before.
(iv) In a school model, a coil wound on a wooden rod lifts far fewer iron clips than the same coil wound on an iron nail.
(v) After a long shift, the crane magnet's coil feels warm.
questions.a: (i) The electromagnet attracts magnetic materials such as iron; aluminium is not attracted, so the magnet also sorts the scrap. (ii) More turns in the coil make the electromagnet stronger. (iii) A larger current makes a stronger magnetic field, so the electromagnet becomes stronger. (iv) An iron core makes an electromagnet much stronger; wood gives no such help. (v) The wire of the coil offers resistance to the current, which turns some electrical energy into heat: the heating effect of electric current.
s: (i) Iron is attracted, aluminium is not
(ii) More turns give a stronger electromagnet
(iii) More current gives a stronger electromagnet
(iv) An iron core makes the electromagnet stronger
(v) Resistance of the coil wire turns electrical energy into heat

questions.q: Household appliances such as electric kettles and electric irons contain a rod or a coil of wire that gets heated when current flows through it. What is this rod or coil called?
questions.a: A heating element
o: A heating element
An electrode
An electromagnet
An electrolyte

questions.q: Why does a nichrome wire become warm when an electric current passes through it?
questions.a: It opposes the flow of current, and this resistance turns some electrical energy into heat.
o: It opposes the flow of current, and this resistance turns some electrical energy into heat.
It stops the current completely, so all the trapped electricity is turned into heat.
The current makes a magnetic field around it, and that field itself warms up the wire.
A chemical reaction between the wire and the air all around it produces the extra heat.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: I. Resistance  II. Heating effect of electric current  III. Heating element  IV. Nichrome wire
Column II: A. The rod or coil of wire inside a heating appliance  B. The opposition a conductor offers to the flow of current  C. A wire that offers higher resistance than a copper wire of the same size and length  D. The generation of heat in a conductor due to the flow of electric current
questions.a: I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-C
o: I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-C
I-D, II-B, III-A, IV-C
I-B, II-D, III-C, IV-A
I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B

questions.q:
A teacher shows the class the glowing coil of an electric room heater and a copper connecting wire. Read these statements.
I. The heater coil gets hot because it offers resistance to the current, and this converts some electrical energy into heat.
II. Copper is used for the connecting wire because it offers higher resistance than a nichrome wire of the same size and length.
III. Two heater coils made of the same material, carrying current for the same time, must produce the same heat, since the heat depends on the material alone.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.q: True or False? 'Overheating in an appliance can damage plugs and sockets, where plastic parts may melt.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. When an electric current passes through a conductor, it gets heated (the heating effect of electric current). When this heating becomes too much, the plastic parts of plugs and sockets may melt, and it may even lead to fires; that is why safety devices are placed in household circuits.
s: States True
Overheating from the heating effect can melt plastic parts or even cause fires

questions.q: (a) What is the heating effect of electric current? (b) Name two household appliances that work on the heating effect of electric current.
questions.a: (a) The generation of heat in a conductor when an electric current flows through it. (b) Any two of: electric room heater, electric stove, electric kettle, electric iron, water heating immersion rod, hair dryer.
s: (a) Heat produced in a conductor by the flow of current
(b) Two correct appliances

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'Nichrome is used for the coils of heaters because it is a poor conductor that blocks the current completely, and that is what makes the heat.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that nichrome offers a high resistance, higher than a copper wire of the same size and length, and that resistance is what turns some electrical energy into heat. He is wrong that it blocks the current completely: nichrome is a conductor and current does flow through it. If no current flowed, no heat would be produced at all.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: high resistance (more than copper) turns electrical energy into heat
Wrong part: current does flow through nichrome; with no current there is no heating

questions.q:
For each device below, say whether it works mainly on the heating effect or the magnetic effect of electric current.
(a) Electric iron
(b) Electric bell
(c) Water heating immersion rod
(d) Loudspeaker
(e) Electric stove
questions.a: (a) Heating effect: its heating element gets hot. (b) Magnetic effect: the book lists electric bells among its applications. (c) Heating effect: its rod is a heating element that heats the water. (d) Magnetic effect: the book lists loudspeakers among its applications. (e) Heating effect: its heating element gets hot, and can be seen glowing red hot.
s: (a) Electric iron: heating effect
(b) Electric bell: magnetic effect
(c) Immersion rod: heating effect
(d) Loudspeaker: magnetic effect
(e) Electric stove: heating effect

questions.q:
A power station near Korba sends electricity to two towns through long wires. For one full week, both lines ran all the time. Line to Town P: 5000 units sent, 4750 units received. Line to Town Q: 5000 units sent, 4600 units received. The difference on each line was lost along its wires. Both lines use wires of the same material and the same thickness, but the line to Town Q is longer. The amount of current in each line was not recorded.
(a) Which effect of electric current causes this loss of energy in the wires?
(b) Work out the units lost on each line, and each loss as a percentage of the units sent.
(c) Name the factor, from those the chapter lists for the heat generated in a wire, that the data tells you is different for the two lines, and say whether the results fit it.
(d) An engineer says: 'These figures prove that the longer line loses more only because it is longer.' Do the figures prove this? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The heating effect of electric current: the wires' resistance turns some electrical energy into heat. (b) Line P: 5000 - 4750 = 250 units lost, 250/5000 = 5%. Line Q: 5000 - 4600 = 400 units lost, 400/5000 = 8%. (c) Material, thickness and duration are the same, so length is the factor that differs; the longer line lost more, which fits length affecting the heat. (d) No. The heat also depends on the magnitude of the current, and the current in each line was not recorded; Town Q may have drawn a larger current. The figures fit the idea, but they cannot prove that length alone caused the difference.
s: (a) Heating effect of current (resistance turns energy into heat)
(b) 250 units (5%) and 400 units (8%)
(c) Length differs; the longer line lost more, which fits
(d) Not proved: current also affects heat and was not recorded

questions.q: Under a teacher's supervision, the same nichrome wire is tested three times, cooling fully between tests. Test X: 1 cell for 30 s. Test Y: a battery of 2 cells for 30 s. Test Z: a battery of 2 cells for 60 s. Which order runs from the most heat generated to the least?
questions.a: Z, Y, X
o: Z, Y, X
Y, Z, X
X, Y, Z
Z, X, Y

questions.q: In a Voltaic cell, what are the two metal rods that are partly dipped in the liquid called?
questions.a: Electrodes
o: Electrodes
Electrolytes
Heating elements
Magnetic poles

questions.q: Which pair of objects can serve as the two electrodes of a home-made Voltaic cell?
questions.a: A copper wire and an iron nail
o: A copper wire and an iron nail
Two copper wires of the same kind
A copper wire and a plastic straw
An iron nail and a wooden stick

questions.q: In Tara's lemon cell, the copper wire is the positive terminal and the iron nail is the negative terminal. She joins a small lamp between them and it glows. Which statement describes the current in the outside circuit?
questions.a: It flows from the copper wire, through the lamp, to the iron nail.
o: It flows from the copper wire, through the lamp, to the iron nail.
It flows from the iron nail, through the lamp, to the copper wire.
It flows out of both electrodes into the lamp and stops there.
It flows out of the lemon juice into the lamp and back again.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A Voltaic cell that has been lighting a lamp for a long time can stop working.
Reason (R): Over time, the chemicals in a Voltaic cell get used up.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'An LED joined to a working chain of lemon cells will glow whichever way round its two wires are connected.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Current passes through an LED only when its positive terminal (the longer wire) is connected to the positive terminal of the battery and its negative terminal (the shorter wire) to the negative terminal. If the LED does not glow, its connections have to be reversed.
s: States False
LED glows only with its longer wire to the positive terminal; otherwise reverse it

questions.q: A lemon cell is made by pushing two different objects into a juicy lemon, a little apart, and it can make an LED glow. (a) Name the two objects that act as the electrodes. (b) What acts as the electrolyte, and what does it do?
questions.a: (a) The copper wire and the iron nail. (b) The lemon juice is the electrolyte; it helps to conduct electricity between the electrodes.
s: (a) Copper wire and iron nail
(b) Lemon juice, which helps conduct electricity

questions.q: Neel has four juicy lemons, each with a copper wire and an iron nail pushed into it a little apart, and he has joined them to one another as his teacher showed. He wants them to light one LED. (a) Between which two points should he connect the LED? (b) He connects it there, but the LED stays dark although the lemons are fresh. What should he try first, and why?
questions.a: (a) Between the copper wire of the first lemon and the iron nail of the last lemon. (b) Reverse the LED's connections. Current passes through an LED only when its positive terminal (longer wire) is joined to the positive terminal of the battery and its negative terminal (shorter wire) to the negative terminal.
s: (a) First lemon's copper wire and last lemon's iron nail
(b) Reverse the LED: it passes current only when its longer wire goes to the positive side

questions.q: Dhruv says: 'A Voltaic cell is like a water tank. Electricity is poured into it when it is made, and it simply flows out until the tank is empty.' Is his idea right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the cell can supply electricity only for a time: over time it stops working and is called dead. He is wrong about where the electricity comes from: nothing is poured in; the electricity is produced by a chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte, and the cell goes dead because these chemicals get used up. (A verdict of 'wrong' is also accepted if it gives this chemical-reaction reason.)
s: Verdict: partly right (or 'wrong' if the chemical-reaction reason is given)
Right part: the cell works only for a time, then goes dead
Wrong part: electricity is produced by a chemical reaction, and the cell dies when the chemicals are used up

questions.q:
A science teacher in Nashik set up a cell in a glass jar: a copper strip and an iron strip, a little apart, partly dipped in salt solution, joined by wires to a small lamp. The class kept a log. Day 1: lamp bright. Day 4: lamp bright. Day 7: lamp dim. Day 9: lamp dark. On Day 9, Raghav took the lamp out and joined it to a fresh dry cell: it glowed brightly.
(a) In this jar, which parts are the electrodes and which is the electrolyte?
(b) What produced the electricity that lit the lamp on Day 1?
(c) What does Raghav's test on Day 9 show?
(d) The class wants the lamp to glow again on Day 10. Should they buy a new lamp or set up a fresh cell? Justify using the log.
questions.a: (a) The copper strip and the iron strip are the electrodes; the salt solution is the electrolyte. (b) A chemical reaction between the metal strips and the salt solution. (c) The lamp is not faulty, since it glows on a fresh cell; so the jar cell is what has stopped working. (d) They should set up a fresh cell. The log shows the light fading from bright to dim to dark over the days, which fits the chemicals getting used up until the cell is dead, and Raghav's test shows the lamp still works, so a new lamp would not help.
s: (a) Copper and iron strips are electrodes, salt solution the electrolyte
(b) Chemical reaction between the strips and the solution
(c) The lamp works, so the jar cell has stopped working
(d) Set up a fresh cell: fading shows chemicals used up, and the lamp is fine

questions.q:
Simran built a chain of lemon cells with copper wires and iron nails. Her teacher told her that in each lemon the copper wire is the positive terminal. Read the five sentences in her report and, for each, say whether it is correct; correct any that are wrong.
(a) 'The lemon juice and the copper wire are the two electrodes.'
(b) 'A salt solution could be used instead of lemon juice.'
(c) 'The current comes out of the iron nail end, goes through the LED and enters the copper wire end.'
(d) 'When my LED did not glow at first, it proved that my lemons were dead.'
(e) 'The electricity comes from a chemical reaction between the metals and the lemon juice.'
questions.a: (a) Wrong: the two electrodes are the copper wire and the iron nail; the lemon juice is the electrolyte. (b) Correct: the book says salt solutions may be used instead of lemon juice. (c) Wrong: current flows from the positive terminal (the copper wire end) through the circuit to the negative terminal (the iron nail end). (d) Wrong: an LED glows only when joined the right way round, so she should first reverse its connections; a dark LED does not prove the lemons are dead. (e) Correct: a chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte produces the electricity.
s: (a) Wrong: electrodes are copper wire and iron nail; juice is the electrolyte
(b) Correct: salt solution can replace lemon juice
(c) Wrong: current flows from the copper (positive) end through the LED to the nail (negative) end
(d) Wrong: the LED may be reversed; reverse it before judging the cells
(e) Correct: chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte

questions.q: Which of these is a single-use cell that has to be disposed of once it is used up?
questions.a: A dry cell in a torch
o: A dry cell in a torch
A mobile phone battery
A laptop battery
An inverter battery

questions.q:
Match each cell or battery in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: I. Voltaic cell  II. Dry cell  III. Rechargeable battery  IV. Lemon cell
Column II: A. Two metal rods of different materials partly dipped in a liquid electrolyte in a glass or plastic container  B. A zinc container, a central carbon rod and a thick moist paste; used only once  C. Can be charged and reused many times, but slowly wears out  D. A copper wire and an iron nail as electrodes, with fruit juice as the electrolyte
questions.a: I-A, II-B, III-C, IV-D
o: I-A, II-B, III-C, IV-D
I-D, II-B, III-C, IV-A

questions.q: Answer briefly about the structure of a dry cell. (a) Which part of a dry cell acts as its negative terminal? (b) Which part acts as its positive terminal? (c) What surrounds the carbon rod inside the cell?
questions.a: (a) The zinc container. (b) The carbon rod at the centre, covered with a metal cap. (c) The paste-like electrolyte (a thick moist paste).
s: (a) Zinc container
(b) Carbon rod with a metal cap
(c) Paste-like electrolyte

questions.q:
A shop sells three kinds of batteries: a laptop battery, an inverter battery and a torch dry cell. Read these statements.
I. The laptop battery and the inverter battery can both be recharged and reused many times, though they are very different in size.
II. Of the three, the torch dry cell saves the most money over time, because it never needs charging.
III. Even the inverter battery will slowly wear out after being charged and used many times.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A dry cell is called 'dry' because its electrolyte is a thick moist paste and not a liquid.
Reason (R): A dry cell is a single-use cell, which has to be disposed of once it is used up.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a rechargeable battery? (b) Name one device that uses a rechargeable battery.
questions.a: (a) A battery that can be recharged and reused multiple times. (b) Any one of: mobile phone, watch, laptop, tablet, camera, inverter, electric vehicle.
s: (a) Can be recharged and reused many times
(b) One correct device

questions.q: Mehul says: 'Dry cells replaced Voltaic cells because Voltaic cells could not produce any electricity that was of use.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Wrong. A Voltaic cell does produce electricity, by a chemical reaction between its electrodes and its liquid electrolyte, and it can light a lamp; the book calls it an important discovery. Dry cells are widely used instead because Voltaic cells, with a liquid electrolyte in a glass or plastic container, are not convenient for everyday use, whereas a dry cell has a thick moist paste in place of the liquid.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
A Voltaic cell does produce electricity by a chemical reaction (an important discovery)
The real reason is convenience for everyday use: a liquid in a container against a paste in a dry cell

questions.q:
A family in Hubballi uses single-use dry cells in three devices. Kitchen weighing scale: 2 cells, replaced once every 12 months. Torch for power cuts: 2 cells, replaced every 3 months. Child's toy train: 3 cells, replaced every week. (Take a year as 12 months or 52 weeks.) The family can afford rechargeable batteries for only one device this year.
(i) Work out how many dry cells each device uses up in a year.
(ii) Find the total number of dry cells the family throws away in a year.
(iii) Choose the device that should get rechargeable batteries first, and give the reason from the chapter.
(iv) Name one device for which a single-use dry cell is still a sensible choice, using the data.
questions.a: (i) Scale: 2 cells. Torch: 2 x 4 = 8 cells. Toy train: 3 x 52 = 156 cells. (ii) 2 + 8 + 156 = 166 cells a year. (iii) The toy train: it uses up 156 of the 166 cells. Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times, so they would prevent the most wastage and save the most money here. (iv) The kitchen weighing scale: it uses only 2 cells a year, so single-use cells cause little waste there.
s: (i) 2, 8 and 156 cells
(ii) 166 cells in all
(iii) Toy train first, since reusable batteries cut the most waste and cost
(iv) The weighing scale, using only 2 cells a year

questions.q:
Ramesh drives an e-rickshaw in Varanasi. Its battery is charged from the mains every night and he drives about 70 km every day. He noted how far the e-rickshaw could go on one full charge. Year 1: 80 km. Year 2: 72 km. Year 3: 60 km. A new battery is costly, and the charging point at his stand allows an extra midday charge for a fee.
(a) What type of battery does the e-rickshaw use, and what does that allow Ramesh to do every night?
(b) By how many km did the distance on one charge fall from Year 1 to Year 3, and what percentage of the Year 1 distance is that?
(c) Why does the distance on one charge keep falling?
(d) In Year 3, should Ramesh buy a new battery or keep the old one and take a midday charge? Using the data, give one point in favour of each choice and then decide.
questions.a: (a) A rechargeable battery, which can be recharged and reused many times, so he can charge it every night. (b) 80 - 60 = 20 km; 20/80 x 100 = 25%. (c) Rechargeable batteries do not last forever; after being charged and used many times they slowly wear out. (d) In Year 3 one charge gives 60 km, 10 km short of his 70 km day. Keeping the old battery and paying for a midday charge avoids the cost of a new battery now; a new battery would cover his 70 km on one charge again (Year 1 gave 80 km) and save the daily fee and time. Either decision is accepted if it uses the 10 km shortfall: for example, buy a new battery because the range will keep falling.
s: (a) Rechargeable battery, reused after each charge
(b) 20 km, which is 25%
(c) Rechargeable batteries slowly wear out after many charges
(d) Uses the 10 km shortfall, gives a point for each choice and decides

questions.q:
Compare a single-use dry cell in a torch with the rechargeable battery in a mobile phone on these five points.
(1) How each produces electric current.
(2) What is done with each once its charge is used up.
(3) What slowly happens to the phone battery after it has been charged and used many times, and what its owner notices after a year or two.
(4) Which of the two causes more wastage and costs more over time, and why.
(5) The phone battery, too, does not last for ever. Using (3) and (4), explain why a phone used every day still runs on a rechargeable battery rather than on single-use cells.
questions.a: (1) Both generate electric current because of chemical reactions taking place inside them. (2) The dry cell is disposed of; the phone battery is recharged and reused. (3) It slowly wears out, so after a year or two it needs charging more often. (4) Single-use dry cells: each used-up cell is thrown away and a new one must be bought, whereas a rechargeable battery prevents wastage and saves money over time. (5) Daily use would use up single-use cells again and again, each one thrown away; the rechargeable battery wears out only after being charged and used many times, so over that time it wastes far less and costs less.
s: (1) Both make current by chemical reactions
(2) Dry cell disposed of; phone battery recharged and reused
(3) Phone battery slowly wears out and needs charging more often
(4) Dry cells cause more waste and cost; rechargeables prevent waste and save money
(5) Wears out only after many charges, so far less waste than a stream of single-use cells
